## Overview

We explore demographic (age, marital, job, education) and financial health (default, balance, housing, loan) variables against term deposit subscription, using the training split only.

```{r}
set.seed(522)
#### Load libraries
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
library(tidymodels)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
#### Load data
bank_df <- read_csv('../data/processed/bank_train.csv')

head(bank_df)
```

## Target variable

```{r}
#### TARGET: term deposit subscription
bank_df |>
  rename(is_deposit = y) |>
  count(is_deposit) |>
  mutate(perc = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 2))
```

The target is imbalanced: only about 12% of clients subscribed.

# Part 1: Demographic variables

```{r}
#### Filter the columns age, marital, job, education and the target column y
bank_demo_df <- bank_df |> select(age, marital, job, education, y) |>
  rename(is_deposit = y)

head(bank_demo_df)
```

## Age

```{r}
#### AGE
bank_demo_df |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    q1 = quantile(age, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    q3 = quantile(age, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(age, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r}
ggplot(bank_demo_df, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = 'lightgrey') +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Number of clients",
    title = "Distribution of client age"
  )
```

Age is right-skewed, ranging from 18 to 95 with a median of 39.

```{r}
bank_demo_df |>
```
```{r}
  mutate(age_group = cut(
```

# Summary of findings

- **Demographics:** age (U-shaped) and job show the biggest differences; education and marital status matter less.
- **Financial health:** having any loan or a default is associated with lower subscription; higher balance is associated with slightly higher subscription.

## Method

- @ANH add in the analysis of the variables here, and tie the writing in with the paragraph below in preprocessing.

### Preprocessing

We evaluated whether eight client characteristics and the previous marketing campaign outcome could predict term deposit subscription more effectively than a majority-class baseline. The client characteristics were age, marital status, occupation, education, credit default, average yearly account balance, housing loan, and personal loan. The ninth predictor, `poutcome`, records the previous campaign outcome and is available before the current call. We used the project's existing training and test split from the UCI Bank Marketing dataset and treated subscription as the positive class.

## Jonah additions below:

We chose to use a classification model using a Logistic Regression with all nine predictors. To predict whether a client would accept the term deposit, we used 5-fold cross validation to select the classification threshold that maximized mean F1. We checked across a range of possible thresholds below 0.5 due to the heavily imbalanced classes in our dataset. We found that a threshold of 0.15 was optimal among the thresholds tested. Because the threshold was selected using only training-data folds, the test set gives an unbiased estimate of performance.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Read in training data
train_df <- read_csv("../data/processed/bank_train.csv")

training_data <- train_df|>
  select(age, marital, job, education, default, balance, housing, loan, poutcome, y)|>
  mutate(y = factor(y, levels = c("yes","no")))

predictor_cols <- c(
  "age", "marital", "job", "education", "default", "balance",
  "housing", "loan", "poutcome")
model_cols <- c(predictor_cols, "y")

# preprocessor
preprocessor <- recipe(y ~ ., data = training_data) |>
  step_dummy(marital, job, education, default, housing, loan, poutcome) |>
  step_normalize(age, balance)

# logistic regression
logistic_model <- logistic_reg() |>
  set_engine("glm") |>
  set_mode("classification")

pipe_logistic <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(preprocessor) |>
  add_model(logistic_model)

# 5-fold cross validation
folds <- vfold_cv(training_data, v = 5, strata = y)
cv_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, recall, precision, f_meas, roc_auc)

logistic_cv <- fit_resamples(
  pipe_logistic,
  resamples = folds,
  metrics = cv_metrics,
  control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE))

preds <- collect_predictions(logistic_cv)
thresholds <- seq(0.05, 0.50, by = 0.05)

# Precision, recall, and F1 at each threshold
multi_metrics <- metric_set(f_meas, precision, recall, accuracy)

threshold_full <- map(thresholds, \(t) {
  preds |>
    mutate(.pred_class = factor(if_else(.pred_yes >= t, "yes", "no"),
                                levels = c("yes", "no"))) |>
    group_by(id) |>
    multi_metrics(truth = y, estimate = .pred_class) |>
    group_by(.metric) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(.estimate, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
    mutate(threshold = t)
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```

Table (x). The 10 thresholds, ranked according to highest mean F1 score. The table shows the mean F1, precision, recall, and accuracy scores.

```{r}
threshold_full |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = mean) |>
  arrange(desc(f_meas)) |>
  select(Threshold = threshold,
         `F1 (%)` = f_meas,
         `Precision (%)` = precision,
         `Recall (%)` = recall,
         `Accuracy (%)` = accuracy) |>
  mutate(across(-Threshold, \(x) 100 * x)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, align = "c")
```

```{r}
# Test data evaluation
test_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/bank_test.csv")
# Predict on test data
logistic_fit <- fit(pipe_logistic, data = training_data)

# Adjust the threshold to 0.15
logistic_prob <- predict(logistic_fit, test_data, type = "prob")$.pred_yes
actual_yes <- test_data$y == "yes"
logistic_yes <- logistic_prob >= 0.15

accuracy = mean(logistic_yes == actual_yes)
precision = mean(actual_yes[logistic_yes])
recall = mean(logistic_yes[actual_yes])

# Calculate F1 and other metric scores
scores <- rbind(
  "Logistic regression" = c(
    accuracy = accuracy,
    precision = precision,
    recall = recall,
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  )
)
```

Table \[y\]. F1, Precision, Recall, and Accuracy of the final model on the test data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bank-test
#| tbl-cap: "Test-set accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for logistic regression at the 0.15 classification threshold."
#| echo: false

kable(data.frame(
  Model = rownames(scores),
  F1 = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "f1"]),
  Precision = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "precision"]),
  Recall = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "recall"]),
  Accuracy = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * scores[, "accuracy"]),
  check.names = FALSE,
  row.names = NULL
))
```

Test performance was consistent with cross-validation (F1 35.07% vs. 35.56%), suggesting the model did not overfit (Tables x and y). However, the model is still miscategorizing many clients. The confusion matrix (Table Z) shows that the model has more false negatives than true positives. A false negative means a likely subscriber is never called, so the bank loses a sale and the client misses a product that suited them.Additionally, the model also has a large number of false positives, which may be harmful to the bank if resources are scarce and efficient allocation is needed.

Table Z. The confusion matrix of model performance on test data at the 0.15 threshold level. Rows are the predictions, while columns are the true class.

```{r}
test_preds_class <- tibble(
  y = factor(test_data$y, levels = c("yes", "no")),
  .pred_class = factor(if_else(logistic_prob >= 0.15, "yes", "no"),
                       levels = c("yes", "no"))
)

cm_test <- conf_mat(test_preds_class, truth = y, estimate = .pred_class)
cm_test
autoplot(cm_test, type = "heatmap")
```

While there is promise in this model as a tool to build a more targeted call list to match clients with term deposits, it still requires more work. The logistic regression model did show that information available before a marketing call can help identify clients who are likely to subscribe to a term deposit. However, even using a threshold of 0.15 to maximize the F1 score, recall was only 44.61%, meaning the model still missed 55.39% of the clients who would have invested in term deposits. While tuning on a slightly finer grid may help to improve our score metrics, it is likely our predictor variables are may not be carrying a strong enough signal. Logistic regression assumes that age and account balance have linear relationships with the log-odds of subscription and that predictor effects are additive on the log-odds scale. These assumptions may miss nonlinear patterns or interactions among client characteristics.

Additionally, we evaluated the model on one test split, so its performance may differ in later campaigns. The data source (Moro et al., 2014) is also limited to Portugeuse banking clients from the period of 2008-2013. This specific time and location sample, which includes the 2008 Financial Crisis, may affect applicability to other countries and/or time periods.

A follow-up study could evaluate the model on a later campaign and ask how many subscribers it identifies when the bank can contact only a fixed number of clients.

**OLD below:**

### Stratified five-fold cross-validation

Logistic regression is suitable for the binary outcome because it estimates the probability that each client subscribes. We fitted an unpenalized logistic regression using all nine predictors and used a fixed classification threshold of 0.50.

We used the same five stratified folds for both workflows to keep the subscription rate similar across folds. We recorded accuracy and recall using the models' default class predictions. With `yes` as the first outcome level, recall measures how many actual subscribers each model correctly identified.

```{r}
# Confusion matrix from CV predictions at the chosen threshold
chosen_threshold <- 0.50

cv_preds_class <- preds |>
  mutate(.pred_class = factor(if_else(.pred_yes >= chosen_threshold, "yes", "no"),
                              levels = c("yes", "no")))

cm_cv <- conf_mat(cv_preds_class, truth = y, estimate = .pred_class)
cm_cv
autoplot(cm_cv, type = "heatmap")
summary(cm_cv)   # accuracy, precision, recall, F1, etc. in one table
```

### Test-set evaluation

We fitted both models on the full training set and evaluated them on the original test set. We classified a client as a subscriber when the predicted probability was at least 0.50. Accuracy measures the proportion of all clients classified correctly. Recall measures the proportion of actual subscribers identified, which is important when the bank wants to reach potential subscribers.

```{r}

logistic_fit <- fit(pipe_logistic, data = training_data)

test_data <- read_csv("../data/processed/bank_test.csv")

logistic_prob <- predict(logistic_fit, test_data, type = "prob")$.pred_yes

actual_yes <- test_data$y == "yes"
logistic_yes <- logistic_prob >= 0.15

precision <- mean(actual_yes[logistic_yes])
recall <- mean(logistic_yes[actual_yes])

scores <- rbind(
  "Logistic regression" = c(
    accuracy = mean(logistic_yes == actual_yes),
    precision = precision,
    recall = recall,
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  )
)
```

## Results

@tbl-bank-cv summarizes accuracy and recall across the five training folds. Logistic regression achieved a mean accuracy of 89.16%, compared with 88.30% for the majority-class baseline. The larger improvement was in recall. On average, logistic regression identified 15.22% of actual subscribers across the folds, while the baseline identified none because it predicted non-subscription for every client.

As shown in @tbl-bank-test, logistic regression achieved 89.61% test accuracy, compared with 88.30% for the majority-class baseline. The main improvement was in recall. As shown in @fig-bank-test-recall, logistic regression identified 184 of 1,058 actual subscribers (17.39% recall), while the baseline identified none (0.00% recall).

```{r}
#| label: fig-bank-test-metrics
#| fig-cap: "Test-set accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for logistic regression at the 0.15 classification threshold."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: false

metric_plot_data <- data.frame(
  metric = factor(
    c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"),
    levels = rev(c("Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"))
  ),
  percent = 100 * unname(scores["Logistic regression", c("accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1")])
)

ggplot(metric_plot_data, aes(x = percent, y = metric)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue", width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f%%", percent)),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 20),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Test-set score (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## Discussion

The logistic regression model showed that information available before a marketing call can help identify clients who are likely to subscribe to a term deposit. On the test set, the model achieved 89.61% accuracy and identified 184 of the 1,058 actual subscribers (17.39% recall). The majority-class baseline achieved 88.30% accuracy and identified no subscribers. We expected the baseline to achieve high accuracy because most clients did not subscribe. Its zero recall shows why accuracy alone gives an incomplete picture when the bank's goal is to reach potential subscribers.

The improvement in recall could help the bank build a more targeted call list. At the fixed 0.50 threshold, however, the model still missed 874 of the 1,058 actual subscribers. Its practical value depends on how many calls the bank can make, the cost of those calls, and the value of reaching additional subscribers.

Logistic regression assumes that age and account balance have linear relationships with the log-odds of subscription and that predictor effects are additive on the log-odds scale. These assumptions may miss nonlinear patterns or interactions among client characteristics. We evaluated the model on one test split, so its performance may differ in later campaigns. A follow-up study could evaluate the model on a later campaign and ask how many subscribers it identifies when the bank can contact only a fixed number of clients.
